atole.name: Ātōlli (atole)
atole.summary: Nahuatl name for a traditional hot maize-based beverage of Mexican origin, sometimes flavored with vanilla, cinnamon, or chocolate and eaten alongside tamales.

pulque.name: Pulque
pulque.summary: A milky, sour, fermented alcoholic drink made from agave sap, traditional in central Mexico for millennia; once sacred and restricted, it became widely popular after the Spanish conquest, peaking in the late 19th century.

agave-americana.name: Maguey (Agave americana)
agave-americana.summary: A flowering plant native to Mexico and Texas, also called maguey or American aloe, widely cultivated worldwide though not closely related to true aloes.

nixtamalization.name: Nixtamalization
nixtamalization.summary: A process of soaking and cooking maize in an alkaline solution such as limewater, which improves its nutrition and flavor and makes it possible to form dough (masa).

chapulines.name: Chapulines
chapulines.summary: Grasshoppers of the genus Sphenarium eaten as a snack in parts of Mexico, especially Oaxaca, seasoned with garlic, lime and chili.

maguey-worm.name: Maguey worm
maguey-worm.summary: Either of two species of edible caterpillar that infest maguey (agave) plants, still eaten as a delicacy in parts of Mexico.

acocil.name: acocil
acocil.summary: A small crayfish species native to Mexico, traditionally boiled or baked and eaten in tacos by pre-Columbian Mexicans; still a subsistence food today.

lake-texcoco.name: Lake Texcoco
lake-texcoco.summary: A former saline lake in the Valley of Mexico whose island city, Tenochtitlan, became the Aztec capital; it was mostly drained after the Spanish conquest.

moctezuma-ii.name: Moctezuma II
moctezuma-ii.summary: Ninth emperor of the Aztec Empire, reigning from 1502 or 1503 until his death in 1520 during the Spanish conquest of Tenochtitlan led by Hernán Cortés. Under him the empire reached its greatest territorial extent.

tututepec.name: Tututepec
tututepec.summary: A Mesoamerican archaeological site on the Oaxaca coast that was capital of a tributary Mixtec empire from about the 12th to the early 16th century, ruling influence over more than 25,000 square kilometers at its height.

mixtec.name: Mixtec
mixtec.summary: Indigenous Mesoamerican peoples of Oaxaca, Puebla and Guerrero, Mexico, whose civilization lasted from about 1500 BCE until the Spanish conquest in 1523.

comal-cookware.name: Comal
comal-cookware.summary: A smooth, flat griddle used across Mexico and Central America to cook tortillas, toast spices and sear meat, often handed down through generations.

zapotec-peoples.name: Zapotec peoples
zapotec-peoples.summary: An Indigenous people of Mexico, numbering 400,000 to 650,000 today and concentrated mainly in Oaxaca, descended from a pre-Columbian civilization with a unique writing system.

ta-no.name: Taíno
ta-no.summary: Indigenous people of the West Indies, part of the Arawak group, who lived in agricultural societies led by caciques and were the first New World peoples encountered by non-Norse Europeans.

james-delbourgo.name: James Delbourgo
james-delbourgo.summary: A historian at Rutgers University whose book Collecting the World, on Hans Sloane's collections that led to the British Museum's founding, won four prizes.

otomi.name: Otomi
otomi.summary: An Indigenous people of central Mexico numbering over 667,000 in 2015, with a language showing wide regional diversity and many different names for themselves.

toltec.name: Toltec
toltec.summary: A pre-Columbian Mesoamerican culture centered at Tula, Mexico, that reached prominence from about 950 to 1150 AD and was regarded by the later Aztecs as their cultural predecessor.

nahuatl.name: Nahuatl
nahuatl.summary: A language of the Uto-Aztecan family spoken in central Mexico since at least the 7th century CE, once the prestige language of the Aztec Empire.

chichen-itza.name: Chichen Itza
chichen-itza.summary: A large Maya city in Yucatán, Mexico, that flourished from about 600 to 900 AD, blending Maya and central Mexican architectural styles, possibly reflecting a diverse population.

puuc.name: Puuc
puuc.summary: A hilly region in Yucatán, Mexico, and the name of the Maya architectural style that flourished there, peaking in the Terminal Classic period.

richard-diehl.name: Richard Diehl
richard-diehl.summary: American archaeologist and scholar of pre-Columbian Mesoamerica, known for extensive work on the Olmec civilization of Mexico's Gulf Coast.

mesoamerican-postclassic-period.name: Postclassic period
mesoamerican-postclassic-period.summary: The final period of independent Mesoamerican civilization, roughly 900 to 1521 CE, marked by urbanization, commerce and migrations, ending with Spanish colonization.

t-ll-n.name: Tōllān
t-ll-n.summary: Nahuatl name meaning roughly 'place of the reeds,' used for the capital cities of Teotihuacan and, later, the Toltec capital Tula, and applied generally to great cities.

macuahuitl.name: Macuahuitl
macuahuitl.summary: A Mesoamerican sword lined with obsidian blades sharper than steel razors, used as a standard close-combat weapon since at least the first millennium CE by the Aztec, Maya and other civilizations.

tenochtitlan.name: Tenochtitlan
tenochtitlan.summary: The Aztec capital built on an island in Lake Texcoco, founded around 1325, that grew into the largest city in the pre-Columbian Americas before its capture in 1521.

tetzcoco-altepetl.name: Tetzcoco
tetzcoco-altepetl.summary: A major Acolhua city-state on Lake Texcoco in the Valley of Mexico, one of the three members of the Aztec Triple Alliance and, after Tenochtitlan, among the largest cities in central Mexico before the Spanish conquest.

tlacopan.name: Tlacopan
tlacopan.summary: A Tepanec/Mexica city-state on the western shore of Lake Texcoco, one of the three cities in the Aztec Triple Alliance that ruled central Mexico from 1428.

valley-of-mexico.name: Valley of Mexico
valley-of-mexico.summary: A large basin in the highlands of central Mexico that was home to pre-Columbian civilizations including Teotihuacan and the Aztec Empire, and now contains Mexico City.

azcapotzalco-altepetl.name: Azcapotzalco
azcapotzalco-altepetl.summary: A pre-Columbian city-state in the Valley of Mexico, capital of the Tepanec empire, said to have been founded by Chichimecs around 995 CE.

axayacatl.name: Axayacatl
axayacatl.summary: Sixth tlatoani of Tenochtitlan and emperor of the Aztec Triple Alliance, who lived from about 1449 to 1481.

sierra-de-las-navajas.name: Sierra de las Navajas
sierra-de-las-navajas.summary: A mountain range in central Mexico and one of the most important obsidian sources in Mesoamerica, its green obsidian used for over 3,000 years by societies including Teotihuacan and Tenochtitlan.

pur-pecha-empire.name: Purépecha Empire
pur-pecha-empire.summary: A pre-Columbian state covering roughly today's Michoacán, Mexico, and nearby areas, the second-largest in Mesoamerica by the Spanish conquest; founded in the early 14th century and conquered by Spain in 1530.

dresden-codex.name: Dresden Codex
dresden-codex.summary: A Maya screenfold book from the Chichén Itzá region, dated to the 11th or 12th century, containing astronomical, astrological and medical tables; long thought the oldest surviving Americas book.

maya-codex-of-mexico.name: Maya Codex of Mexico
maya-codex-of-mexico.summary: A pre-Columbian Maya screenfold manuscript, formerly known as the Grolier Codex, one of only four surviving Maya codices; confirmed in 2018 to date from 1021-1154 CE, making it the oldest known book in the Americas.

eight-deer-jaguar-claw.name: Eight Deer Jaguar Claw
eight-deer-jaguar-claw.summary: A powerful Mixtec ruler in 11th-century Oaxaca (1063–1115), known from the Codex Zouche-Nuttall and other manuscripts, named after his day of birth.

codex-bodley.name: Codex Bodley
codex-bodley.summary: A Mixtec pictographic manuscript from around 1500 recording history, named after Oxford's Bodleian Library where it has been kept since the 17th century.

codex-zouche-nuttall.name: Codex Zouche-Nuttall
codex-zouche-nuttall.summary: A pre-Columbian Mixtec pictorial manuscript, now in the British Museum, recording the genealogies, alliances, and conquests of 11th- and 12th-century Tilantongo rulers.

la-mixteca.name: La Mixteca
la-mixteca.summary: A cultural and political region in western Oaxaca and neighboring Puebla and Guerrero, Mexico, home to two-thirds of the country's Mixtec people.

maya-script.name: Maya script
maya-script.summary: The Maya civilization's writing system, the only Mesoamerican script fully deciphered, combining logograms with syllabic glyphs; used from the 3rd century BCE until the Spanish conquest.

tilantongo.name: Tilantongo
tilantongo.summary: A Mixtec city-state and political center in the Mixteca Alta region of what is now Oaxaca, Mexico, during the Postclassic period.

codex-vindobonensis-mexicanus-i.name: Codex Vindobonensis Mexicanus I
codex-vindobonensis-mexicanus-i.summary: A 14th-century accordion-folded Mixtec manuscript recording ritual, calendrical, and genealogical information.

amate.name: Amate
amate.summary: A type of bark paper made in Mexico since precontact times, used for Mayan and Aztec codices and records, whose production survived the Spanish conquest in remote mountain villages.

ficus-cotinifolia.name: Ficus cotinifolia
ficus-cotinifolia.summary: A fig tree species native to dry tropical Mexico and Central America, whose bark was pounded to make amate paper.

j-eric-s-thompson.name: J. Eric S. Thompson
j-eric-s-thompson.summary: An English Mesoamerican archaeologist, ethnohistorian and epigrapher (1898–1975) who dominated Maya studies, especially the study of the Maya script, into the 1960s.

linton-satterthwaite.name: Linton Satterthwaite
linton-satterthwaite.summary: American Maya archaeologist and epigrapher (1897–1978) linked to the University of Pennsylvania, known for work at Caracol, Piedras Negras, Cahal Pech and Xunantunich.

clive-ruggles.name: Clive Ruggles
clive-ruggles.summary: British astronomer and archaeologist (born 1952) appointed in 1999 to what was then the world's only professorship in archaeoastronomy, at the University of Leicester.

zelia-nuttall.name: Zelia Nuttall
zelia-nuttall.summary: An American archaeologist who discovered forgotten pre-Columbian manuscripts, deciphered the Aztec calendar stone, and challenged the accepted site of Francis Drake's Pacific landing.

cholula-mesoamerican-site.name: Cholula
cholula-mesoamerican-site.summary: A pre-Columbian Mesoamerican city near modern Puebla, Mexico, and a key religious center home to the largest pyramid structure by volume in the world.

palenque.name: Palenque
palenque.summary: A Maya city-state in southern Mexico, inhabited from around 226 BCE to 799 CE, known for fine architecture and inscriptions and for its ruler Pakal the Great, whose tomb was found there.

sacred-cenote.name: Sacred Cenote
sacred-cenote.summary: A water-filled sinkhole at Chichen Itza where the Maya deposited valuables and human sacrifices to the rain god Chaac, confirmed by 20th-century excavations.

k-iche-people.name: Kʼicheʼ people
k-iche-people.summary: An Indigenous Maya people of Guatemala whose highland states peaked during the Postclassic period (c. 950–1539); their name, meaning 'many trees', gave rise to the word Guatemala.

kaqchikel-people.name: Kaqchikel
kaqchikel-people.summary: An indigenous Maya people of Guatemala's highlands and southern Mexico, today Guatemala's third largest Maya group.

tlatoani.name: Tlatoani
tlatoani.summary: The historical title of a dynastic ruler of a Nahuatl city-state, who also served as high priest and military commander; the Aztec emperor held the higher title 'huey tlatoani'.

tepanec.name: Tepanecs
tepanec.summary: A Mesoamerican people who settled in the Valley of Mexico in the late 12th or early 13th century, closely related to the Aztecs and speaking the same Nahuatl language.

itzcoatl.name: Itzcoatl
itzcoatl.summary: Fourth king of Tenochtitlan, ruling from 1427 to 1440, who broke the Mexica free from Tepanec rule and founded the Aztec Empire's Triple Alliance with Tetzcoco and Tlacopan.

coyoac-n.name: Coyoacán
coyoac-n.summary: A borough of Mexico City and former Aztec-era village whose name means 'place of those who own coyotes'; the Spanish used it as their headquarters and briefly as the first capital of New Spain, 1521 to 1523.

cuernavaca.name: Cuauhnahuac
cuernavaca.summary: The Nahuatl name, meaning 'near the trees,' for the city later Hispanicized as Cuernavaca; Hernán Cortés and Bernal Díaz del Castillo recorded other Spanish spellings of it.

quetzalc-tl.name: Quetzalcoatl
quetzalc-tl.summary: A major Aztec deity, the 'Feathered Serpent', linked to wind, the planet Venus, the sun, learning and the priesthood; later accounts conflated him with a legendary Toltec ruler.

c-catl-topiltzin.name: Ce Acatl Topiltzin
c-catl-topiltzin.summary: A mythologised 10th-century Toltec ruler in Aztec tradition, later a cultural hero often confused with the god Quetzalcoatl; legend credits the exiled Toltec Ce Acatl Topiltzin with founding Cuzcatlán in El Salvador.

huemac.name: Huemac
huemac.summary: In Mexica legend, the last king of the semi-mythical Toltec state before the fall of its capital Tula, though whether he was a real historical figure remains debated.

xaltocan.name: Xaltocan
xaltocan.summary: Pre-Columbian city-state and island in the Valley of Mexico's Lake Xaltocan, originally settled by the Otomi people before being resettled by Nahuatl speakers.

moctezuma-i.name: Moctezuma I
moctezuma-i.summary: Second Aztec emperor, ruling Tenochtitlan from 1440 to 1469, who consolidated and expanded the empire and made Tenochtitlan the dominant power in the Aztec Triple Alliance.

nonoalca.name: Nonoalca
nonoalca.summary: A Mesoamerican people who played a major role in Toltec culture, forming most of the devotees of Quetzalcoatl at Tula and later scattering across the region.

chichimeca.name: Chichimeca
chichimeca.summary: A term the Aztecs and Spanish used for nomadic and semi-nomadic peoples of north-central Mexico, comparable to "barbarian," who fiercely resisted Spanish expansion.

chapultepec.name: Chapultepec
chapultepec.summary: A large forested park in Mexico City centered on Chapultepec Hill, a retreat for Aztec rulers and later home to Chapultepec Castle.

toluca-valley.name: Toluca Valley
toluca-valley.summary: A valley in central Mexico west of the Valley of Mexico, historically a buffer region between the Aztec and Purépecha empires and now home to the city of Toluca.

cemanahuac.name: Cemanahuac
cemanahuac.summary: The Aztec name for their world, corresponding to the modern term Mesoamerica.

altepetl.name: Altepetl
altepetl.summary: Local, ethnically based city-state political unit of pre-Columbian Nahuatl-speaking societies, each with its own ruler, origin story, and sense of identity.

mexica.name: Mexica
mexica.summary: A Nahuatl-speaking people of the Valley of Mexico who ruled the Triple Alliance, commonly called the Aztec Empire, and founded Tenochtitlan in 1325 before Spanish conquest ended their rule in 1521.

nahuas.name: Nahuas
nahuas.summary: An Indigenous people of Mexico, the largest such group there, including the Aztec (Mexica) and their historic rivals the Tlaxcallans, who speak Nahuatl.

aztl-n.name: Aztlán
aztl-n.summary: The mythical ancestral homeland of the Aztec peoples, cited in colonial-era sources as the starting point of their migration to central Mexico; its real location, if any, is debated.

tezozomoc-azcapotzalco.name: Tezozomoc
tezozomoc-azcapotzalco.summary: Tepanec ruler of Azcapotzalco from around 1353 to 1426, remembered as a military and political leader who expanded Tepanec dominance over the Valley of Mexico.

pipiltin.name: Pipiltin
pipiltin.summary: The noble social class of the Mexica (Aztec) Empire, ranked above commoners and serving as ambassadors, army officers and priests.

tl-loc.name: Tláloc
tl-loc.summary: The Aztec god of rain, fertility, and water, feared for his power over hail, thunder, and lightning, and associated with caves, springs, and sacred mountains.

tzintzuntzan-michoac-n.name: Tzintzuntzan
tzintzuntzan-michoac-n.summary: Town in Michoacán, Mexico, that served as the capital of the Tarascan (Purépecha) state until its conquest by the Spanish in the 1520s.

mesoamerican-language-area.name: Mesoamerican language area
mesoamerican-language-area.summary: A group of languages from families such as Mayan, Uto-Aztecan and Oto-Manguean, spoken across Mesoamerica, that share syntactic, lexical and phonological traits despite their different origins.

zaachila.name: Zaachila
zaachila.summary: A powerful Mesoamerican Zapotec city in what is now Oaxaca, Mexico, and the final Zapotec capital after Monte Albán fell.

isthmus-of-tehuantepec.name: Isthmus of Tehuantepec
isthmus-of-tehuantepec.summary: A narrow strip of land in Mexico marking the shortest route between the Gulf of Mexico and the Pacific Ocean, once a major overland transport route before the Panama Canal opened.

mixe-people.name: Mixe
mixe-people.summary: An Indigenous Mesoamerican people of the eastern highlands of Oaxaca, Mexico, who have kept their own language, Mixe, to this day.

huave-people.name: Huave people
huave-people.summary: An Indigenous people of Mexico who have lived on the Isthmus of Tehuantepec for over 3,000 years, preceding the Zapotec in the area.
